source_text: ΕΓΚΩΜΙΟΝ Εἰς τὸν ἐν ἁγίοις πατέρα ἡμῶν Εὐστάθιον ἀρχιεπίσκοπον Ἀντιοχείας τῆς μεγάλης. αʹ. Σοφός τις ἀνὴρ καὶ φιλοσοφεῖν εἰδὼς, τῶν ἀνθρω πίνων πραγμάτων τὴν φύσιν μετὰ ἀκριβείας κατα μαθὼν, καὶ ἐπιγνοὺς αὐτῶν τὴν σαθρότητα, καὶ ὡς οὐδὲν ἔχει πιστὸν, οὐδὲ βέβαιον, παραινεῖ κοινῇ πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις πρὸ τελευτῆς μὴ μακαρίζειν μη δένα. Οὐκοῦν ἐπειδὴ τετελεύτηκεν ὁ μακάριος Εὐστάθιος, μετὰ ἀδείας αὐτὸν ἁπάσης ἐγκωμιάσαι λοι πὸν δυνάμεθα· εἰ γὰρ πρὸ τελευτῆς οὐ δεῖ μακαρίζειν οὐδένα, μετὰ τὴν τελευτὴν ἀνεύθυνος ἐπὶ τῶν ἀξίων ὁ μακαρισμὸς γένοιτ' ἄν. Καὶ γὰρ παρῆλθε τὸν εὔρι πον τῶν βιωτικῶν πραγμάτων, ἀπηλλάγη τῆς ταρα χῆς τῶν κυμάτων, πρὸς τὸν εὔδιον καὶ ἀτάραχον κατ.40 έπλευσε λιμένα, οὐχ ὑπόκειται τῇ τοῦ μέλλοντος ἀδηλίᾳ, οὐδέ ἐστιν ὑπεύθυνος καταπτώσει, ἀλλὰ καθάπερ ἐπὶ πέτρας τινὸς καὶ ὑψηλοῦ σκοπέλου νῦν ἑστὼς καταγελᾷ τῶν κυμάτων ἁπάντων. Οὐκοῦν ἀσφαλὴς ὁ μακαρισμὸς, ἀνεπίληπτον τὸ ἐγκώμιον· οὐ γὰρ δέδοικε μεταβολὴν, οὐχ ὑποπτεύει μετάπτωσιν. Ἡμεῖς μὲν γὰρ οἱ ἔτι ζῶντες, καθάπερ οἱ ἐν μέσῳ πελάγει σαλεύοντες, πολλαῖς ὑποκείμεθα ταῖς μεταβολαῖς· καὶ καθάπερ ἐκεῖνοι νῦν μὲν εἰς ὕψος αἴρονται τῶν κυμάτων κορυφουμένων, νῦν δὲ πρὸς αὐτὸν καταφέρονται τὸν βυθόν· ἀλλ' οὔτε τὸ ὕψος ἀσφαλὲς, οὔτε ἡ ταπείνωσις μόνιμος· ὑδάτων γάρ ἐστι ῥεόντων καὶ οὐχ ἱσταμένων ταῦτα ἀμφότερα· οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων πραγμάτων οὐδὲν βέβαιον καὶ ἑστὼς, ἀλλὰ πυκναὶ αἱ μεταβολαὶ καὶ ὀξύῤῥοποι. Ὁ μὲν ὑπὸ τῆς εὐημερίας πρὸς τὸ ὕψος ἐπήρθη, ὁ δὲ ὑπὸ δυσπραγίας εἰς πολὺ κατηνέχθη βάθος· ἀλλὰ μήτε ἐκεῖνος φυσάσθω, μήτε οὗτος ταπεινούσθω· ταχίστην γὰρ ἕκαστος δέξεται τὴν μετα βολήν· ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐκεῖνος ὁ πρὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν μεταστὰς, ὁ πρὸς τὸν ποθούμενον ἀπελθὼν Ἰησοῦν, ὁ πρὸς χω ρίον ἐλθὼν καθαρὸν θορύβων, ἔνθα ἀπέδρα ὀδύνη καὶ λύπη καὶ στεναγμός. Οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκεῖ μεταβολῆς εἰ κὼν, οὐκ ἔστι τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα, πάντα δὲ πεπη γότα καὶ ἀκίνητα, πάντα βέβαια καὶ ἱδρυμένα, πάντα ἄφθαρτα καὶ ἀθάνατα, πάντα ἀκήρατα καὶ εἰς ἀεὶ διαμένοντα. Διὰ τοῦτό φησι, Πρὸ τελευτῆς μὴ μακάριζε μηδένα. Διὰ τί; Ἄδηλον γὰρ τὸ μέλ λον, καὶ ἡ φύσις ἀσθενής· ἡ προαίρεσις ῥᾴθυμος, ἡ ἁμαρτία εὐπερίστατος, πολλαὶ αἱ παγίδες· Ἐπί γνωθι γὰρ, φησὶν, ὅτι ἐν μέσῳ παγίδων διαβαίνεις· ἐπάλληλοι οἱ πειρασμοὶ, πολὺς ὁ τῶν πραγμάτων ὄχλος, καὶ διηνεκὴς τῶν δαιμόνων ὁ πόλεμος, καὶ συνεχεῖς αἱ τῶν παθῶν ἐπαναστάσεις· διὰ ταῦτα, Πρὸ τελευτῆς μὴ μακάριζε μηδένα, φησίν. Οὐκοῦν μετὰ τελευτὴν μακαρίζειν ἀσφαλὲς τὸν ἄξιον· μᾶλλον δὲ οὐχ ἁπλῶς μετὰ τελευτὴν, ἀλλὰ τελευτὴν τοιαύτην, ὅταν μετὰ στεφάνου τὸν βίον ᾖ καταλύσας τις, ὅταν μετὰ ὁμολογίας καὶ πίστεως ἀνυποκρίτου. Εἰ γὰρ τοὺς ἁπλῶς τελευτήσαντας ἐμακάρισέ τις, πόσῳ μᾶλλον τοὺς οὕτω τελευτήσαντας; Καὶ τίς ἐμακάρισε, φησὶ, τοὺς ἁπλῶς τελευτήσαν τας; Ὁ Σολομὼν, Σολομὼν ἐκεῖνος ὁ πάνσοφος· μὴ γὰρ ἁπλῶς παραδράμῃς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, ἀλλ' ἐννόησον τίς ἦν, καὶ πῶς βεβιωκὼς, καὶ μετὰ πόσης ἀδείας καὶ ἀνέσεως τὸν ὑγρὸν καὶ ἀταλαίπωρον βίον ἔζη.
thought_title: Praise is safe only after death
orientation: Chrysostom opens his encomium by arguing that since Scripture forbids calling anyone blessed before death, Eustathius can now be praised without risk because he has died and reached a secure harbor.
pass_a_gloss: A certain wise man, one who knew how to live virtuously, having learned with precision the nature of human affairs, and having recognized their rottenness, and that they have nothing trustworthy nor stable, advises all people in common not to call anyone blessed before death. Therefore, since the blessed Eustathius has died, we are now able with all freedom to praise him; for if one must not call anyone blessed before death, after death the blessing of the worthy would be without liability. For he has passed through the strait of the affairs of life, he has been freed from the disturbance of the waves, he has sailed into the calm and untroubled harbor, he is not subject to the uncertainty of the future, nor is he liable to a fall, but just as if standing now upon some rock and high crag he laughs at all the waves. Therefore the blessing is safe, the encomium is beyond reproach; for it does not fear change, it does not suspect a reversal. For we who are still living, just as those tossing in the middle of the open sea, are subject to many changes; and just as those are now lifted to the height when the waves crest, and now are carried down to the very deep; but neither is the height safe, nor is the lowliness lasting; for both these things are of waters that flow and do not stand; so indeed also in human affairs nothing is stable and standing, but the changes are frequent and swift. One man is lifted to the height by prosperity, another is carried down into a great depth by misfortune; but let neither that one be puffed up, nor let this one be humbled; for each will receive the change most swiftly; but not that one who has departed to heaven, who has gone away to the longed-for Jesus, who has come to a place pure of disturbances, where pain and grief and groaning have fled away. There is no image of change there, there is no shadow of turning, but all things are fixed and immovable, all things are stable and established, all things are incorruptible and immortal, all things are undefiled and enduring forever. Because of this he says, Before death call no one blessed. Why? For the future is uncertain, and nature is weak; intention is sluggish, sin is easily encompassing, the snares are many; For know, he says, that you walk in the midst of snares; the temptations are successive, the crowd of affairs is great, and the war of the demons is continuous, and the uprisings of the passions are constant; because of these things, Before death call no one blessed, he says. Therefore after death it is safe to bless the worthy one; rather not simply after death, but after such a death, when someone has ended his life with a crown, when with confession and unfeigned faith. For if someone blessed those who simply died, how much more those who died in this way? And who, he says, blessed those who simply died? Solomon, that all-wise Solomon; for do not simply pass by the man, but consider who he was, and how he had lived, and with how much freedom and relaxation he lived the soft and effortless life.

choices.english: one who knew how to live virtuously
choices.why: The glossary requires φιλοσοφία as 'virtuous life'; the verbal form here describes Solomon's skill in the disciplined life, not abstract philosophy.
rejected: one who knew how to philosophize

choices.why: The word denotes decay and unsoundness; 'rottenness' preserves the vivid physical metaphor Chrysostom uses for the instability of human affairs.
The Euripus is a narrow, turbulent channel; 'strait' conveys the dangerous passage of life's affairs that Eustathius has now crossed.
The noun denotes a collapse or downfall; 'fall' keeps the moral and spiritual sense of a lapse that the dead are no longer liable to.
The word means a shadow cast by turning; 'shadow of turning' echoes the biblical language of change and preserves the image of instability.
The word means unmixed, pure, uncorrupted; 'undefiled' captures the purity and permanence of the heavenly state.

bible_refs.note: ἀπέδρα ὀδύνη καὶ λύπη καὶ στεναγμός

pass_b_english: A certain wise man, one who knew how to live virtuously, had studied the nature of human affairs with precision. He recognized their rottenness, and saw that they contain nothing trustworthy or secure. So he offers this counsel to all people alike: do not call anyone blessed before his death. Since the blessed Eustathius has now died, we can at last praise him with complete confidence. For if no one should be called blessed before death, then after death the blessing of those who deserve it is beyond reproach. He has crossed the strait of life's affairs. He has been freed from the turmoil of the waves. He has sailed into the calm, untroubled harbor. He is no longer subject to the uncertainty of the future, nor is he liable to a fall. Instead, as if standing now on some rock or high crag, he laughs at all the waves. So the blessing is secure, and the praise is beyond reproach. It does not fear change; it does not suspect reversal.

We who are still living are like people tossed about in the middle of the open sea. We are subject to many changes. Just as they are now lifted high when the waves crest, and now carried down to the very depths—yet neither the height is secure nor the low point lasting, for both belong to waters that flow and do not stand still—so also in human affairs nothing is firm or fixed. Changes are frequent and swift. One person is lifted to the heights by prosperity; another is carried down to a great depth by misfortune. But let neither one be puffed up, nor the other be humbled. Each will receive change very quickly. But not that man who has departed to heaven, who has gone to the Jesus he longed for, who has come to a place pure of disturbances, where pain and grief and groaning have fled away. There is no image of change there, no shadow of turning. All things are fixed and immovable, all things secure and established, all things incorruptible and immortal, all things undefiled and enduring forever.

This is why he says, “Do not call anyone blessed before his death” (Ecclesiastes). Why? Because the future is uncertain, and human nature is weak. The will is sluggish, sin easily surrounds us, and the snares are many. “Know,” he says, “that you are passing through the midst of snares” (Ecclesiastes). Trials come one after another. The press of affairs is great. The war of the demons is unceasing. The uprisings of the passions are continuous. For these reasons, he says, “Do not call anyone blessed before his death.” So after death it is safe to call the worthy person blessed. Or rather, not simply after death, but after a death of such a kind—when someone has ended his life with a crown, when he has ended it with confession and unfeigned faith. For if someone called blessed those who simply died, how much more those who died in this way?

And who, you ask, called blessed those who simply died? Solomon—that all-wise Solomon. Do not pass over the man lightly. Consider who he was, how he had lived, and with what freedom and ease he lived that soft and effortless life.

problems.why: ῥᾴθυμος means 'sluggish/lazy,' not 'careless.' The sense is human will/choice is weak or lax, not negligent.

last_rejected.why: προαίρεσις means 'intention/choice' (glossary term), not 'will' in modern sense; 'sluggish' for ῥᾴθυμος is weak—means 'negligent/lax/idle'
last_rejected.ruling: προαίρεσις as 'will' and ῥᾴθυμος as 'sluggish' are within normal semantic range; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.why: εὐπερίστατος means 'easily encircled/ensnaring' (active sense: sin lies in wait, Heb 12:1), not 'surrounds us' which makes sin's action sound gentle
last_rejected.ruling: 'Easily surrounds us' captures εὐπερίστατος ('easily encircling'); active sense preserved adequately.
